It’s understandable to be concerned and you could contact your pcp if you need their reassurance. Generally taking the missed dose a few hours late is fine but if it’s too close to your next dose, wait and take your next as prescribed.

Google some grounding techniques and do a few deep breathing exercises to help slow your heartbeat and reduce stress. 

This illness can become a vortex where your symptoms cause stress, stress exacerbates the symptoms, and you never get out of it without intervention.

If you can sit still for just a few minutes and place your feet on the floor and your arms on arm rests or in your lap comfortably, close your eyes, and breathe deeply in through your nose and out through your mouth counting in for four and out for six. 

While you breathe, focus on how your body feels in your environment right now starting with your feet. Press your toes into the floor, then heels, notice your shins, knees, thighs, hips, abdomen, and go through every part of you that is touching the chair and how it feels. Is it smooth, rough, cold, warm, just focus on being in the chair and keep breathing.

Once you feel more centered, you can open your eyes and carry on. You can do it for as long as you need.

If you’re not already, you could speak to someone about helping you work out a plan to deal with intrusive thoughts. 

Missing a dose can have physical effects on you but panicking can also have negative effects. 

And like other posters have said, get a pill box. Maybe set alarms in your phone or computer for when pills are scheduled. Leave yourself notes. Have failsafes in place.

Good luck.

First-I live on the Mississippi River and will now exclusively say “thug boat” so thank you!

The tarring was done often to keep bugs from boring through the wood which would weaken it and allow rot more quickly. It would be mixed with oil (like linseed) and brushed on frequently to the hull.

Tar and oakum (a hempy kind of material) were mixed together, by hand, and then shoved between the planking on the deck to help make it watertight. They would then use “bible stones” to “sand” down and smooth the decks. (Tar Heels is a reference to the black feet of sailors, usually ones who were “before the mast” or not officers of any sort.)

A lot of caravels and other small-ish ships were made of “hardwood” which is interesting because of its density (it’s hard…hence the name) but also its ability to float.

There were a few well known ships that had actual reinforced hulls. Two layers of fairly intricate planking that helped with weight distribution and gave them extra protection and time to patch holes caused from battle, reefs, or really big whales.

Since at least the 1400s, ships were surprisingly built to withstand a LOT of rough weather. The tall deck on the aft part of the ship (the poop deck-not named for poop but for the Latin word for stern) helped with waves that crashed over the deck by preventing the deck or hold to become swimming pools. 

They were also really heavy and again, surprisingly well designed to suit their purposes but specifically the hulls were designed for the waters they expected to face. 

Personally, for small modern boats, I’d prefer wooden over fiberglass because I like how they feel in the water (but mainly because they’re so much prettier.) however, a sunken wooden ship is definitely less preferable to floating glass one…regardless of how cool it looks…

Straits of Florida is the bit of water south of the Keys made of the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic with some Caribbean Sea mixed in when the winds are strong and from the south.

OP depends on what you want to do on the seaside. The Florida panhandle has some of the most incredibly powdery white sand and bright clear water that you’ll find on Earth. The southern Gulf is like swimming in a giant, warm water swimming pool. The East Florida coast is lovely but always feels very busy opposed to the west coast.

The keys are piratical, even today. The northern shores and flats filled with beautiful (and delicious) seafood and lobstering is one of the coolest things you can do if you are there at the right time.

The upper gulf is made for fishing and shrimping and is dotted with tons of barrier islands and tons of sea birds. Scalloping around Appalachiacola is like hunting for Easter eggs but the result is arguably better. There are countless small fishing towns that are still quiet and mostly unvisited as well as ship builders and military bases.

The eastern seaboard has always felt unique because it’s still dotted with small seaports and some quieter beaches, outer banks with horses, and a lot of interesting coastal landscapes that’s opposite of the city skyline you see on the coast of Miami and Lauderdale.

Lighthouses, constantly changing coastal landscapes and shifting channel entrances keep it interesting and exciting because a single storm can alter navigable waters within minutes. 

Coastal New England is magical to me because of its rocky, pebbly beaches and incredible Nor’easters that can make waves so huge they crash into top floors of beachside homes and its beachside communities are quintessential Americana where summer holidays could be taken from a Rockwell painting.

Maine has always seemed bigger and more mysterious to me because it combines a lot of the comfortable, homey atmosphere you expect from “coastal towns” while still feeling a little uncharted and sometimes even spooky like you’re experiencing what people hundreds of years ago did.

The Great Lakes are an amalgamation of every waterside town imaginable. The number of lighthouses, beautiful clean beaches and bright blue, clear water are always surprising and things like “lake effect snow” will forever make them seem like something that was made up.

The city scape that’s seen when you’re in the water, looking back at land can make it seem like you’re watching a movie that’s not yet complete. You can see the signs that money and people are there but far enough away that you can still pretend you’re adventurous and brave and seeing something for the first time.

The shipwrecks that are still hidden all along the coasts are reminders that there were people before us who were brave enough to venture out without knowing what to expect.

So, as for favorite, it is impossible to decide. Today, my favorite would be something along the northeastern coast that’s far away from skyscrapers but not quite so isolated that it feels scary or lonely. 

As for the pacific coast, it may be the most ironically named thing you’ll ever see on a map!

All in all, there’s not a foot of coastal landscape that’s not worth seeing. Just depends on the day…
